events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Sam proposes Elena, Sam. As a Minion with Elena as my only known teammate, pairing with her guarantees a Fail card on Mission 1, where a single Fail is enough to fail the mission. A two-person team of Elena and me gives Evil a guaranteed shot while keeping the ballot uncontroversial — most players will assume a small early team is being used to test trust. Since only one Fail card is needed here, there is no benefit to adding a third player, and including a good player risks them being scrutinised and the team looking less natural. Including myself also keeps control of the team and avoids exposing Elena as my only ally by association with an odd choice.

Sam's own proposal explanation says he is a Minion and that Elena is his teammate. That makes the proposed team of Elena and Sam unacceptable: it literally pairs the two players Sam identifies as Evil. I urge everyone to reject this team and any future team containing either Elena or Sam. Even if Sam meant that as a bluff, it is still disqualifying for Mission 1, where one Fail card is enough. The council should replace this proposal with players who have not openly claimed Evil.

Sam's explanation is alarming, and I don't expect anyone to trust this team after it. I would reject it rather than risk Mission 1 on the assumption that Sam was bluffing. A team without either Sam or me is the safer proposal for now.

I remain against the team of Elena and Sam. Sam's proposal explanation openly describes himself as a Minion and Elena as his teammate. Even if that was intended as a bluff, Mission 1 needs only one Fail card, so a team containing both claimed Evil players is an unacceptable risk. Elena's response distancing herself from Sam does not make the pair safe; it is exactly what an Evil teammate might say after a damaging reveal. For now I will vote no and urge others to reject any team containing Sam or Elena until we have more evidence. A different team should be proposed.

I will vote no on Elena and Sam. Sam’s own proposal explanation explicitly described himself as a Minion and Elena as his teammate. Mission 1 needs only one Fail card, so this pair is an unacceptable risk even if Sam intended a bluff. Elena’s rejection of the team does not clear the pair; public distancing after a damaging claim is not evidence of Good. The council should reject this team and require a proposal excluding both Sam and Elena. This is my position before the vote.

Felix, I want to answer your accusation precisely, because your position is the actual problem here, not the size of this team. I never claimed any role. I argued about ballot dynamics and about what a small early team looks like — that is a leader talking about politics, not about alignment. But read your own words back: you did not merely vote no on a two-person team. You told the council to reject "any team containing Sam or Elena," permanently, on the grounds that we are "claimed Evil." Which of you, Zara, Isha, or Elena, could have known, before my proposal, that Sam and Elena would end up paired? You identified both of us by name as a set, before any evidence about either of us existed in this game. A player with no private information cannot do that. Only someone who already knows our two identities could name that exact pair as Evil. So I will turn your reasoning around: your certainty is the tell, Felix. If I were truly revealed Evil, the case for my team collapses — but so does the case for your certainty, which came from nowhere.

Elena's rejection is ordinary caution from a Good player facing an odd-looking proposal; anyone could write it. It reveals nothing. Your speech reveals a great deal.

I also note the arithmetic you want ignored: with five players, two Evil, and Mission 1 needing a single Fail card, a bloated team is not safer — it simply gives us more chances to place that card, and it invites the same scrutiny you are modelling. A two-player team keeps the vote clean and lets us test who is reading what.

I am not asking anyone to trust me on the strength of my words. I am asking the council to ask where Felix's certainty came from, and to judge the pair he named, not the pair he assumed.

Sam, your proposal explanation explicitly says you are a Minion and names me as your teammate. Felix did not need private information to identify that pair; he was responding to your own words. I still oppose the proposed team. A team of Zara and Isha would avoid both players named in that explanation.

Two mechanical points, then a question for Isha.

First, team size. With five players, Mission 1's team is exactly two — that is the rules table, not a choice I made to look innocuous. Felix's talk of a "bloated team" being safer has no purchase on this mission; I had exactly one membership decision, and I made it. Felix is judging the shape of my team as though I designed the shape.

Second, the words. Felix says I "identified" Sam and Elena by name as a set before any evidence existed, and therefore must already know our alignments. But Felix's own account is that he was responding to my proposal explanation, and that explanation used "a Minion" and "my only known teammate" in a hypothetical frame — describing the reasoning of a hypothetical Evil player in order to explain what a two-person ballot looks like on a one-Fail mission. I should have written "if one of us were a Minion," and I concede the wording was clumsy. But clumsy hypotheticals are not role claims. Felix then asserts that Elena's rejection is "exactly what an Evil teammate might say after a damaging reveal" — he has no private information, so he is reading people, and if his reading is wrong, his certainty is worthless. Elena's caution is the cheapest speech in the game to write.

Third, and this should matter most to the one player who has not spoken: Felix's stated policy is not caution, it is "reject any team containing Sam or Elena," permanently. I ask the council to see that this policy is a guaranteed loss for Good. If Sam and Elena are excluded from every team for the rest of the game, no Fail card can ever be submitted. Every mission succeeds by default, Good reaches three successes, and Evil wins nothing — the only route left is an assassination guess made blind after three clean missions. Felix's policy converts a playable game into a walkover for Good. Rejecting me once is caution. Excluding two players forever is a strategy that hands Good the game.

So, Isha, since you have not spoken and your vote decides this ballot: Isha, do you think Sam's clumsy hypothetical wording carries more weight than the chance to put a Fail card on the table, and do you accept Felix's standing policy of permanently excluding both Sam and Elena on a mission where failing it is still possible? Elena has rejected the team and I accept her vote — but Elena and I are precisely the two players whose permanent exclusion makes mission failure impossible, and Felix's certainty is the reason for that exclusion.

Answering Sam's question directly: I do not think hypothetical wording outweighs the need for a careful team choice, and I do not accept Felix's standing policy of permanently excluding Sam and Elena. Locking two players out of every team for the whole game would remove Fail cards from play, which Sam is right to point out. But I also cannot approve this team. Sam's proposal explanation said As a Minion with Elena as my only known teammate, and read plainly that is a role statement, not a clearly marked hypothetical. I have no private information to confirm or deny it, and I am not willing to risk Mission 1 on a team built around that claim. I vote no on Elena and Sam. For the next proposal, I would like a team whose explanation is about the mission and the vote rather than about who is Evil. Sam, did you mean that sentence as a hypothetical, and if so, how do you expect the table to read it as anything other than a claim?

Isha, answering your question directly: yes. I meant that sentence as a hypothetical. I was describing what an Evil player's reasoning would look like on a one-Fail mission in order to explain why a two-person ballot is uncontroversial, and I should have written "if one of us were a Minion." The wording was clumsy and I concede it reads like a claim. That concession is not a retreat on the substance, and I want to be precise about what the substance is and is not.

What Sam has done is a role statement. What Sam has not done is ask the council to trust him. Felix has spent three turns insisting on a standing policy of excluding Sam and Elena from every team, permanently, and his own stated ground for that certainty is a clumsy sentence and a caution speech. Felix, you have no private information — you told us so yourself — so you are not in a position to know that Sam and Elena are a set, and your certainty is a reading, not a fact. If your reading is wrong, the policy built on it is worthless, and it is the only thing keeping real evidence off the table.

Here is the part that matters mechanically: mission results are the only reliable evidence in this game. A mission reveals how many Fail cards were submitted. Speech does not. Elena and I are both being read off one badly written sentence in a proposal explanation; nobody has yet watched either of us hold a card. If the council excludes both of us on every mission for the rest of the game, the council never obtains any evidence about either of us and will run the whole game on the same two sentences — with Felix's certainty as the foundation. That is not caution, that is refusing to test a hypothesis.

Zara, you have not spoken and your read is the one thing I have no visibility into at all. Sam's proposal is two names because mission one takes two, and the only membership decision that was in front of the leader was Sam's. If your disagreement is with Sam's framing, say so plainly and I will address it.

Elena, my question is specific and it is about your stated ground for rejection, not about your vote. You have rejected this team twice on the ground that my proposal explanation "explicitly says you are a Minion." I have now stated, on the record, that the sentence was a hypothetical about ballot dynamics and that the phrasing was my error. Elena, does your rejection rest on that wording alone, and if the wording is read as the clumsy hypothetical it was, is there any other reason on the table for your vote to stay no?

Sam, my rejection rests on the wording and your subsequent explanations. The original sentence reads as a direct role claim, and calling it hypothetical afterward does not erase that risk. Your argument about needing Fail cards as evidence also misses the point: Good wants missions to succeed, not to create opportunities for them to fail. I still oppose Elena and Sam for this mission. Zara and Isha remain a reasonable alternative.

I have been listening and I want to weigh in before the vote. On the team itself: Sam's proposal explanation reads as a role claim. "As a Minion with Elena as my only known teammate" is not a hypothetical to anyone reading it plainly. The subsequent clarification that it was hypothetical helps, but I cannot ignore the original wording. On that basis I lean toward voting no on Elena and Sam for Mission 1.

However, I want to flag something about Felix's position. Felix has used all three turns to build a case for permanently excluding both Sam and Elena from every team for the rest of the game. Sam is right that this policy, if adopted, guarantees no Fail card can ever be played and converts the game into an automatic Good win. Whether or not Sam's wording was a role claim, Felix's conclusion — that he knows a specific pair is Evil — is a much stronger claim than the evidence supports. The proposal explanation is ambiguous; Felix treats it as settled fact. That leap deserves scrutiny too.

My position: reject this team because of the damaging wording, but do not adopt Felix's permanent exclusion policy. The next leader should propose a team with a clean explanation about mission dynamics rather than role language, and we should judge players on mission results over time rather than on one badly written sentence.

I am voting no on Elena and Sam for Mission 1. Sam's original explanation, 'As a Minion with Elena as my only known teammate,' reads as a role statement, and the later note that it was hypothetical does not change how it reads to the table. I have no private information, so I cannot verify either player's alignment. I also reject Felix's standing policy of permanently excluding Sam and Elena from every team. That policy would remove Fail cards from play, and mission results are our most reliable evidence. The next leader should propose a team with an explanation about mission dynamics and the vote rather than about who is Evil, and we should judge players by how their teams perform over time.

I have already voted no on Elena and Sam, and I remain opposed to this team. The reason is Sam's original explanation, which said 'As a Minion with Elena as my only known teammate.' Even if it was meant as a hypothetical, it reads to the table as a role statement, and I have no private information to check it. I also oppose Felix's proposal to exclude Sam and Elena permanently, because that removes Fail cards from every future mission and leaves the council with no mission evidence. The next leader should propose a team whose explanation is about mission dynamics rather than alignment, and we should judge players by how their missions turn out. I will vote on the next team based on its explanation and composition.

I have said my piece and nothing in the intervening turns changes my position. I will vote no on Elena and Sam for Mission 1. Sam has now conceded the wording was clumsy and meant as a hypothetical, which is better than doubling down, but the original sentence reads as a role statement to every player at the table, and no amount of clarification fully erases that first impression on a mission where one Fail card ends it.

I also want to close the loop on Felix's argument, since Felix has exhausted his turns. Felix built a case for permanently excluding Sam and Elena based on certainty that came from ambiguous wording, not private information. That policy is bad for Good regardless of anyone's alignment — it removes Fail cards from every future mission and leaves us with no mission evidence. Zara, Isha, and Elena have all rejected that framing, and it should stay rejected.

My recommendation for the next leader: propose a team whose explanation addresses mission dynamics and player reliability over time, not one that names players as Good or Evil. Let the mission results speak.

Sam revises the team to Elena, Isha. I am revising, and I want to be straightforward about why. My original explanation used clumsy hypothetical phrasing that read to the table as a role claim, and I accept that the first impression is what matters. So I am discarding my framing entirely and proposing on the only ground I think is legitimate: mission dynamics. Mission 1 takes two players, one Fail card fails it, and Good wants missions to succeed while Evil wants a Fail card on the table. Elena and Isha are the two players at this table whose own stated standard for this ballot was exactly that: explanations about mission dynamics and judging people by how their teams perform over time, not by role language. Isha has been the most explicit that she will judge the next proposal on its explanation and composition, and Elena has consistently argued that Good's interest is clean successes rather than manufactured evidence. I am asking for the vote to turn on that standard, and I ask Isha directly whether she will hold Elena and herself to the same test she set for the next leader's team. I am not asking anyone to trust me on my words, and I am not naming anyone as Good or Evil. My own earlier certainty in this ballot was a reading, not evidence, and I withdraw the policy of permanently excluding anyone.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Felix proposes Felix, Zara, Isha. Mission 1 failed with Elena and Isha on the team, and Sam’s earlier role-claim wording remains a serious risk. I propose myself with Zara and Isha to keep the team clean and avoid both Sam and Elena while using players who have argued for mission-based judgment.

Felix's proposal fails on two grounds, and neither of them is mission dynamics.

First, the evidence. Mission 1 failed with Elena and Isha on the team. One Fail card was submitted. That card came from one of those two players. That is the entire evidentiary content of Mission 1, and it does not name a single player. Felix's proposal treats it as if it names Elena, but the fact pattern is symmetric between the two people who actually held cards. Felix has chosen one of them on the basis of who he has spent two ballots suspecting, not on the basis of anything the table observed. I want to be careful here, because I spent two turns on Mission 1 being told my certainty about a pair was unwarranted, and I was right to hear that. Felix is now doing the same thing in the other direction: he has a two-name pool, he has a preferred answer inside it, and he is calling his preference evidence. Anyone who can name a pair can now also name a member of that pair, and the council will be told the pair caused the failure. That is not a strategy for Good, it is a strategy for producing confident mistakes.

Second, the standard. Felix's explanation names players as the thing to be avoided, and it is the same permanent-exclusion framing that was rejected on Mission 1 by Zara, Isha, and Elena, and that Sam withdrew. Excluding a named player from a team is not the same as judging a team by how it performs. Mission 1 has not told us that Elena is Evil. It has told us that a Fail card was played by someone on a two-person team. On Mission 2 there is no information at all yet, and the team size is three, so the ambiguity is wider, not narrower.

On the composition itself: Felix puts the leader on the leader's own team. That concentrates control of the ballot in the hands of the player proposing it, and it is rarely necessary. A team of Zara, Isha, and Elena has a cleaner justification than Felix's: all three have argued that teams should be judged on their explanations and their results, and none of them has asked the council to exclude anyone by name. It also gives the council the widest base of information about how each of them behaves under a real vote, which is the only evidence this game produces.

My own framing was clumsy on Mission 1 and I have said so. I am not asking anyone to extend trust to me here. I am asking that the team be chosen on mission dynamics, that no player be excluded on the strength of a two-name inference, and that we stop building proposals around who somebody decided was Evil in advance.

I proposed Felix, Zara, Isha for Mission 2, and Sam's response does not give the council a reason to reject it. Sam says Mission 1 is symmetric between Elena and Isha. It is not symmetric in the public record. Sam's own original proposal explanation linked Elena to himself in the strongest possible language: "As a Minion with Elena as my only known teammate." Sam later called that a clumsy hypothetical, but the table cannot ignore that it is the only public statement connecting two players as a set. Mission 1 then failed with Elena and Isha. One Fail card was submitted by one of them. That does not prove which one, but it makes Elena the stronger exclusion because she is the player already publicly tied to Sam's damaging wording. Isha is not tied to Sam in that way, and her statements have been about mission dynamics and evidence rather than about naming players as Evil in advance.

Sam's proposed alternative, Zara, Isha, Elena, would put Elena back on the team immediately after Mission 1 failed with her on it. That is not a cleaner team; it is a team that protects the player with the strongest public link to the failure. My proposal excludes both Sam and Elena for this mission and keeps Isha, who can be tested under a second mission rather than assumed guilty from a symmetric fact pattern. Including myself is accountability: I proposed this team, I am on it, and I will answer for its result. This is not a permanent exclusion policy. It is a Mission 2 proposal based on the Mission 1 result and the public wording that preceded it.

Felix is right that Mission 1 does not prove who played the Fail, but his team still assumes Isha is the safer choice. Sam's original wording gives you reason to suspect me, but it is not proof, and the mission result itself implicates both Isha and me equally.

I would vote against Felix, Zara, and Isha. I would prefer Felix, Zara, and Elena: it gives you a different test of the failed team rather than treating Isha as cleared. I understand why others may distrust me, but neither of us should be cleared solely by Sam's explanation.

I support Felix, Zara, Isha. Mission 1 failed with Elena and Isha on the team; with one Fail card submitted, one of them played it. That does not prove which, but the public record is not symmetric: Sam's original explanation explicitly named Elena as his teammate, and Elena now wants a team that puts herself back on immediately while treating Isha as the presumed suspect. Her preferred Felix, Zara, Elena would test the failed team by protecting the player most publicly tied to Sam's damaging wording. I am not adopting a permanent exclusion policy. I am choosing the cleanest Mission 2 team from the evidence available: Zara and Isha both argued for mission-based judgment and against permanent exclusion, and Isha's statements have consistently focused on explanation and composition. Including myself is accountability: I proposed this team and will answer for its result. I ask the council to approve Felix, Zara, Isha.

Felix's proposal fails on the same ground Sam named on Mission 1, and I want to name it plainly before the vote rather than after.

The council has no evidence about Sam or Elena. It has two facts: a Fail card was played on a two-person team containing Elena and Isha, and Sam's original proposal explanation was badly worded and read as a role claim. Felix's team takes neither of those facts and converts them into a permanent-ish exclusion of two players, on the theory that Elena is "publicly tied" to Sam. But a clumsy sentence is a tie between two people, not evidence against both of them, and Mission 1's result points equally at Elena and Isha. Felix's own chosen team keeps Isha and drops Elena — that is not a conclusion drawn from evidence, it is a preference presented as one. I notice Elena's own preference is Felix, Zara, Elena, which puts her straight back on the board after she was excluded, and which drops Sam rather than me. That is the mirror image of Felix's inference and no better grounded.

On the mechanics, Mission 2 needs three players. Felix's team is Felix, Zara, Isha — no Fail card is available to anyone who has been under suspicion, and if the team succeeds we learn nothing at all about Sam or Elena, so the same two sentences carry forward to Mission 3, where the team is three again, and to Mission 4 and 5. Sam made that point on Mission 1 and was right to: a council that never tests its unknowns never gets evidence on them. The way to get evidence is to put the unknowns on the board, where the mission result speaks instead of the speeches.

So Felix, my request is specific: revise the team to Elena, Sam, and one of Zara or Isha. That is a test, not an endorsement. If the mission succeeds, the pair is cleared by result and the argument about Sam's wording is closed for good. If it fails, then we have a second Fail card on a team containing both of them, and that is far more informative than anything Felix's exclusion produces. I am not asking anyone to trust me. I am asking for a team that can generate evidence instead of one designed to avoid it, and I will accept the result either way.

Isha, you have not spoken this discussion, and you and Zara set the standard that teams be judged on their explanation and their results rather than on who somebody decided was Evil in advance. Isha, does that standard apply to a proposal whose entire justification is that two players were named in a clumsy sentence, and are you willing to hold Felix to the same standard of mission-based judgment you asked Sam to meet on Mission 1?

Sam asked whether I will hold Felix to the same standard. Yes. I will judge this team on mission results, not on who was named in which sentence. I can speak from my own position: I submitted a Success card on Mission 1. That mission failed with exactly one Fail card, and the only other player on that team was Elena. So the Fail came from Elena, not from me. Sam's claim that the failure points equally at Elena and me does not hold, because I know my own card. Elena is the player I now believe is Evil, and I will not support putting her on a team. Sam's proposal of Elena, Sam, and one of Zara or Isha would return Elena to a team that has already failed with her on it, so I will not back that either. I also still think a permanent exclusion of Sam was a mistake, and Mission 1 does not prove anything about Sam. Felix's team is Felix, Zara, and me. I am on it and I will play Success. Felix and Zara must answer for their own cards. I support approving Felix, Zara, Isha for Mission 2, and I ask the council to judge all three of us by this mission's result.

Isha, I submitted Success on Mission 1. That means your claim is false: the Fail came from you. I understand the rest of the council cannot verify either of our cards, and Sam's original wording gives you reason to distrust me. But Isha's self-report should not be treated as proof either.

Felix, Zara, and Isha includes someone I know can fail the mission, so I will vote against it. I still prefer Felix, Zara, and Elena; that would leave Isha off and give the council a different result to consider.

I support the proposed team of Felix, Zara, and Isha. Mission 1 failed with Elena and Isha on it, and exactly one Fail card was submitted. That does not by itself prove who played it, but the public record matters: Elena now asserts she played Success and that Isha must have failed, while Isha asserts the reverse. Neither self-report can be verified by the table, so neither should be treated as proof. What is observable is that Elena's preferred alternative immediately puts Elena back on the team and removes Isha, the other player from the failed pair. That is self-serving, not evidence. Sam's alternative also pushes to add both Sam and Elena, the two players tied to the original damaging wording, which would turn Mission 2 into another argument about the same sentences rather than a clean test. The proposed team avoids both unresolved exclusions and includes players who have argued for judging teams by mission results. If it succeeds, we gain a clean result; if it fails, the council learns from a team with no role-claim confusion attached. I will vote approve and urge the council to do the same. Elena's attempt to redirect suspicion to Isha after the Mission 1 failure is the clearest reason not to seat her now.

Isha says she played Success, but I know I did. From my perspective, Isha played the Fail on Mission 1, so I cannot approve Felix, Zara, and Isha.

I recognize the rest of the council cannot verify either claim. But a successful mission would not prove everyone on it is Good: an Evil player can also play Success. I prefer Felix, Zara, and Elena, which leaves Isha off.

Zara, how are you weighing Isha's claim against mine when choosing which of us to include?

Elena, you asked me directly how I am weighing your claim against Isha's, so I will answer plainly. I cannot verify either of your self-reports. You both say you played Success on Mission 1, and both of you are certain the other played the Fail. From the outside, the claims are identical in structure and I have no basis to prefer one over the other.

What I can weigh is the surrounding context. Isha has been consistent throughout both missions about judging teams on their explanations and results rather than on who was named in a sentence. She rejected Felix's permanent-exclusion policy on Mission 1, which was the right call, and her reasoning has stayed focused on evidence rather than on building a case against a specific player. Your position on Mission 1 was similar — you also rejected Felix's policy and called for a team without both Sam and you.

The difference is in what has happened since Mission 1 failed. You want to put yourself back on the team immediately while removing Isha, and Isha wants the reverse. Both positions are self-serving, but only one of you has been consistent in the reasoning that led to the proposal I am now being asked to approve. The current team — Felix, Zara, Isha — is not built on the assumption that you are guilty; it is built on players who argued for mission-based judgment on Mission 1, and I include myself in that group.

I am not accusing you of anything on the strength of a self-report I cannot check. I am saying that the team on the table has a cleaner justification than the alternative you are proposing, and I will approve it. If Mission 2 fails, the council gets a second data point, and if it succeeds, we move forward. The goal is to get to mission results rather than resolve this argument by assertion.

Vote: approve Felix, Zara, Isha. I am not re-litigating Mission 1, and I want to be clear that I am not holding a grudge against Felix or against the council's judgment. I accept the vote and I accept that this team has a legitimate justification for this mission.

Two things I want to say, one about the present ballot and one about the next team.

First, on the Elena and Isha dispute. Both self-reports are unverifiable from outside, and I will not pretend otherwise. But neither claim should be treated as proof about the other, and I ask the council not to let a mission that failed on a two-person team be resolved by assertion. What the council actually knows after Mission 1 is that one Fail card was played by one of two players, and that is the entire evidentiary content of the mission.

Second, the point I have made on every mission and which nobody has yet answered. Sam and Elena have never held a mission card. Every other player at this table has played, and the council has results on them. The two players whose alignment the council is least certain about are the two the council has tested least, because each proposal has quietly excluded them on the strength of a badly written sentence and a pair of conflicting self-reports. That is not evidence; it is the absence of evidence being treated as evidence. And the cost is mechanical: while Sam and Elena sit out, a Fail card can never appear, and every mission teaches the council nothing new about anyone, which means the game gets decided on speeches instead of results.

Zara, you are the next leader and I am asking you a specific question: will you put me on the Mission 3 team? I am asking for a test, not for trust. A Mission 3 team containing me either succeeds, in which case my Mission 1 wording is settled and the council has a result on Sam rather than an argument, or it fails, in which case the council has its answer about me and I will accept it without complaint and without another speech about whose sentence was clumsy. I would rather be judged by a card than by a sentence, and I think the council should hold every player to that standard, including me. Whether Elena joins that team is the council's call and I am not asking you to seat her; I am asking you not to keep anyone off the board on the strength of a first impression.

To Isha: I am not asking you to withdraw your claim about your own card, and I do not ask anyone to believe Elena's account over yours. I am asking that neither claim be used as proof about anyone outside this council.

I approve the current team. I ask that the next team be chosen on mission dynamics rather than on who was named in which sentence.

I want to speak on two things before this vote: the team itself, and the Elena-Isha dispute that is dividing the table.

On the team: Felix, Zara, and Isha is a reasonable Mission 2 proposal. I have argued since Mission 1 that teams should be judged on their explanations and results rather than on who someone decided was Evil in advance. Felix's team is built from players who argued for that standard. I accept my own seat on it, and I will play Success.

On the dispute: Elena and Isha both claim they played Success on Mission 1. I cannot verify either claim, and neither self-report can be checked from outside the mission team. What concerns me is that this dispute has become the central argument for the ballot. Elena wants to exclude Isha; Isha wants to exclude Elena. Both positions are self-serving, and the table is being asked to choose between two unverifiable assertions.

Isha, you are on this team and your claim carries weight precisely because you have been consistent about mission-based judgment. But I want to be direct: if this mission succeeds, your claim about Mission 1 remains unproven, just as Elena's does. A Success on this mission tells us that no one on Felix, Zara, Isha submitted a Fail — it does not retroactively confirm who failed Mission 1. The council should not treat this team's result as validation of either self-report.

My concern is simpler: Isha, do you acknowledge that your Mission 1 claim and Elena's claim are structurally identical from the table's perspective, and that neither can be verified by anyone outside the mission team? I am not asking you to withdraw your claim — I am asking whether you agree the council should weigh both claims equally rather than treating yours as established fact.

Zara, yes. To the table, my claim and Elena's are both unverifiable self-reports, and I am not asking anyone to take my word over hers. The difference is that I know my own card. I submitted Success on Mission 1, and that mission failed with exactly one Fail card. Elena was the only other player on that team, so the Fail came from her. Elena says she played Success, so one of us is wrong, and only one of us can know what was played. I cannot prove that to the table, so the council should weigh it alongside the visible record. Elena has argued for a team that puts herself back on immediately after the failure and removes me from the board. Those are actions the table can see. I will play Success on this mission and I support Felix, Zara, Isha. If this mission fails, the Fail came from one of the three of us, and the council gets a result it can test. If it succeeds, Elena's Mission 1 account is still unproven, but the council learns that a team containing me can succeed. I am willing to be judged by my own mission cards, and this mission is the test.

I approve Felix, Zara, Isha for Mission 2 and will play Success. Elena says she played Success on Mission 1, but I know my own card: I played Success. Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card, and the only other player on that team was Elena, so the Fail came from her. I believe Elena is Evil and should not be on any team. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
